🔥🇲🇽 <u>LOZOYA BACK IN THE DOCK: COURT REVIVES AGRONITROGENADOS CASE</u>

A federal tribunal just dragged former Pemex chief Emilio Lozoya back into court. The Tercer Tribunal Colegiado unanimously denied his amparo and reactivated the Agronitrogenados case — frozen since August 2023. The numbers never stopped being obscene: Pemex paid $275 million for a fertilizer plant valued at $58 million brand new, and Lozoya allegedly pocketed $3.4 million from AHMSA in 2013. The court ruled that Ancira's reparations deal is no get-out-of-jail card for his co-defendant. The Peña Nieto era's favorite middleman is running out of road.

‍SILENCE: BMW confirms 2027 EV production in Mexico — zero US coverage July 23, 2026 | 💀 📰 BMW will assemble its Neue Klasse EVs — i3 sedan, iX3 crossover — and high-voltage batteries in San Luis Potosí from 2027. One of only four plants worldwide, backed by an €800M expansion. 🔍 US media filed dozens of tariff stories on Mexico this week. Stories on Mexico landing next-generation German EV production: zero.

NATIONAL REVIEW: The End of 'El Mayo' Is Only the Beginning July 23, 2026 | 🔴 📰 El Mayo got life plus a $15B forfeiture. National Review's verdict: "only the beginning." The playbook never updates — jail the boss, declare victory, demand the next escalation. 🇲🇽 Zambada ran Sinaloa for four decades; the cartel didn't miss a beat. Forty years of kingpin removals later, fentanyl is cheaper than ever. NR's answer: more of the same. (Paywalled — headline-level read, no quotes.) Source

‍EL PAÍS: Mexico leads Latin America's pushback against Trump's migrant crackdown July 20, 2026 | 🟢 📰 62 dead in 18 months of ICE operations — 52 in custody. 17 Mexicans, more than any other nationality. Mexico is the only country filing criminal complaints in US courts and state prosecutors' offices; Colombia's incoming president and Venezuela said nothing. 🇲🇽 Sheinbaum also took it to the UN. A rare piece that quotes Mexicans about Mexico. • "Seventeen Mexicans have died, and nothing has happened, not even the slightest apology" • Washington returned Mexico's protest letters: an attempt "to dictate the actions of U.S. government personnel"

‍LATIN TIMES: U.S., Mexico Announce Largest-Ever Financial Crackdown on Jalisco Cartel July 24, 2026 | 🟡 📰 Treasury's largest CJNG action ever: 55 targets — 39 people, 16 companies spanning fuel, tequila, agriculture, construction, furniture. Five months after El Mencho was killed, the cartel has a new boss and OFAC has a new list. 🔍 Two weeks ago ICG reported the crackdown hasn't dented fentanyl flows. Nobody asked Bessent about that. • "the resources it uses to traffic fentanyl, terrorize communities, and threaten American lives"

‍REUTERS: Mexico to see no change from new US tariffs, economy minister says July 23, 2026 | 🟢 📰 Trump hit 60 economies with 10–12.5% "forced labor" tariffs this week. Canada ate 50%. Mexico? 85% of exports stay tariff-free under USMCA, and the 4th review round is set for September. The fight left: autos content. Reuters ran Ebrard's readout straight, no editorializing. • "see no change in the effective tariff that Mexico pays" • "One replaces the other, so tariff treatment is maintained"

🇲🇽🏭 <u>THE MAQUILA MODEL'S BALANCE SHEET: 76% OF WOMEN IN MEXICO'S TEXTILE INDUSTRY WORK INFORMAL</u>

The "Hilando el Cambio" report by the UNIDAS consortium — Fundación Avina, ProDesc, Ethos and Oxfam México — puts numbers on the export model neoliberalism built: in the last quarter of 2025, 76% of women in the garment-maquila industry worked with no contract, against 53% of men.

INEGI's figures: average monthly pay in the industry is 6,666 pesos — but women take home 5,387 while men get 9,282. Women maquila workers earn 42% less, and still carry 52 hours a week of unpaid domestic work against 36 for men.

The industry exports to the world. The women who sustain it have no contract, no IMSS, no pension.

Via El Economista.

🇲🇽🏠 <u>22 OPERATIONS IN ONE WEEK: MEXICO CITY'S ANTI-DESPOJO TASK FORCE RETURNS STOLEN PROPERTIES</u>

Between July 15 and 22, the Mexico City Gabinete Contra Despojos ran 22 interinstitutional operations across 12 of the capital's 16 boroughs, executing judicial orders against organized groups that seize homes through fraud and simulated sales.

In colonia Roma, a fake real-estate purchase was undone and the property restored to its rightful owner. In Narvarte, a tenant with a formal lease — backed by favorable court rulings — got the property back. In Venustiano Carranza, a commercial unit was returned and the rest of the building preventively seized pending forensic investigation.

Led by César Cravioto, coordinating with the capital's prosecutor's office and police. Organized patrimonial crime, met with organized institutions.

🇲🇽🇨🇺 <u>WASHINGTON'S "EXTRATERRITORIAL LAWS": THE LEGAL WEAPON AIMED AT MEXICAN COMPANIES IN CUBA</u>

Title III of the Helms-Burton Act, activated by Trump in 2019, lets US courts sue Mexican, Spanish and Canadian companies that invest in properties Cuba nationalized decades ago. International law recognizes no such power — Washington uses it anyway.

UNAM legal scholar Ruperto Patiño Manffer and lawfare researcher Silvina Romano break it down in Contralínea: the T-MEC era makes the US-Mexico relationship the clearest case of the tension between sovereignty and interdependence — and defending sovereignty requires diversifying international ties.

Romano's summary of how geopolitical lawfare works: "There are always lawyers behind it."
